title: Intramedullary nailing of the tibia
subtitle: Reamed locked nailing of a tibial shaft fracture

sources.org: SPRINT Investigators. J Bone Joint Surg Am 90:2567
sources.title: Randomized trial of reamed and unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Fractures (complex): assessment and management (NG37)
BOAST: Diagnosis and Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Extremities

indications: Displaced or unstable tibial shaft fractures in skeletally mature patients.
Open tibial shaft fractures once debridement is complete and definitive soft-tissue cover can follow immediately.
contraindications: Active infection in the canal or at the entry site.
An open fracture in which definitive soft-tissue cover cannot be achieved at the same time: stabilise temporarily instead.
Very proximal or very distal fractures where a nail cannot control alignment without additional techniques.
preparation: Full-length tibial and fibular radiographs including knee and ankle; CT if there is intra-articular extension.
Neurovascular and compartment assessment documented before anaesthesia.
Consent includes compartment syndrome, malalignment, anterior knee pain, infection, non-union and further surgery.
positioning: Knee flexed over a radiolucent support for an infrapatellar entry, or semi-extended for a suprapatellar entry.
C-arm from the opposite side so anteroposterior and lateral views of the whole tibia are possible.
equipment: Tibial nail system with targeting jig, ball-tipped guidewire, flexible reamers and locking screws.
Reduction aids: pointed reduction clamps, a femoral distractor or blocking screws.
anatomy: The entry point lies just medial to the lateral tibial spine on the AP view and at the anterior edge of the plateau on the lateral view.
The tibial canal is triangular; the anteromedial surface is subcutaneous along its length.
The anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve run on the interosseous membrane; the saphenous nerve and vein lie medially at the ankle.
criticalSafety: Correct entry point on both views is the single biggest determinant of alignment in proximal fractures.
Keep the guidewire centred in the distal fragment on both views before reaming.
Do not ream with a tourniquet inflated: the bone cannot dissipate the heat.
Maintain awareness of compartment syndrome for 48 hours after fixation.
structuresAtRisk: Patellar tendon and articular cartilage at the entry site
Anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve with locking screws
Saphenous nerve and vein at the distal medial screws
Superficial peroneal nerve near the distal lateral screws
commonErrors: A medial entry point in a proximal third fracture, producing valgus and procurvatum.
Distraction at the fracture after locking, a known cause of non-union.
Malrotation, unnoticed because it is not visible on plain images.
complications: Anterior knee pain, particularly after infrapatellar entry.
Deep infection, more frequent after open fractures.
Thermal necrosis from reaming, and fat embolism.
postop: Hourly neurovascular and compartment observations initially, with explicit monitoring if a regional block was used.
Weight-bearing as the construct and fracture pattern allow, usually as tolerated for a stable locked nail.
Thromboprophylaxis per local protocol; wound review; radiographs at follow-up to track union.

steps.emphasis: Knee flexion for infrapatellar entry, or semi-extension for suprapatellar. Check both full-length views before draping.
Restore length, alignment and rotation before the guidewire crosses the fracture. Compare rotation with the other leg.
Ball-tipped guidewire centred in the distal fragment on both views, ending just above the ankle physeal scar.
Compartments of the leg checked and documented now, and the 48-hour observation plan handed over.

step.tibnail.entry.title: Entry point
step.tibnail.entry.why: The nail follows the entry point. An entry that is medial or too distal drives a proximal fracture into valgus and procurvatum and no amount of reaming corrects it.
how: Approach through a patellar tendon split, medial parapatellar incision, or a suprapatellar portal with a protective sleeve.
Place the awl or entry wire just medial to the lateral tibial spine on the AP view and at the anterior edge of the plateau on the lateral view.
Confirm on both views before opening the canal.
pitfalls: Medial entry in a proximal fracture.
Entry too posterior, risking the posterior cortex.

step.tibnail.ream.title: Measuring and reaming
step.tibnail.ream.why: Reaming allows a larger, stiffer nail. SPRINT suggested a possible benefit of reamed nailing in closed fractures, with no difference shown in open fractures.
how: Measure nail length from the guidewire.
Ream in small increments with sharp reamers, advancing slowly, with the fracture held reduced.
Ream slightly beyond the planned nail diameter, per the system technique.
pitfalls: Pushing blunt reamers fast and generating heat.

step.tibnail.insert-lock.title: Nail insertion and locking
step.tibnail.insert-lock.why: Locking controls length and rotation; inserting the nail without losing reduction is what makes the locking worth doing.
how: Insert the nail by hand through the jig while the reduction is held, without forceful hammering.
Seat the nail so it does not protrude above the entry point.
Lock distally freehand using perfect-circle technique, then proximally through the jig; backslap to close any distraction before the second set of screws.
structuresAtRisk: Anterior tibial artery and deep peroneal nerve
pitfalls: Prominent nail at the knee causing pain.
